newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba acknowledges dengue outbreak in eastern city.
newsitem.headline: Cuba acknowledges dengue outbreak in eastern city.

text.p: Cuban authorities said on Wednesday they were fighting an outbreak of dengue fever in the eastern city of Santiago de Cuba and several hundred cases of the mosquito-transmitted tropical disease had been detected.
Diplomatic sources and residents of the city reported the outbreak earlier this week, but officials had previously declined to comment publicly.
The Health Ministry said in a statement that the illness was limited to Santiago, 560 miles (900 km) east of the capital.
It said the outbreak was being contained and, with its long experience of combating such illnesses, Cuba hoped to "eradicate it (the illness) very quickly".
The outbreak was the first in Cuba since dengue epidemics in 1981 and 1977-78. The 1981 epidemic involved several hundred thousand cases and caused 150 deaths.

Dengue fever, transmitted by the Aedes Aegypti mosquito, causes headaches and body aches, high fever and a rash and usually lasts for about one week. In its most serious form, which is rare, it can cause haemorrhages and can be fatal.

The ministry's statement, published in the ruling Communist Party daily Granma, did not give a figure for the number of cases reported in Santiago, beyond saying there were "several hundred". But it said numbers of new cases were falling thanks to efforts to eradicate the carrier mosquito.
The statement also said there had been few serious cases in adults.

There have been rumours among Cubans that about 10 people have died in the outbreak -- possibly people who had some other ailment and then contracted dengue. It was not possible to confirm this, and the ministry did not mention deaths.
The statement said a national campaign was under way to wipe out the carrier mosquito and urged citizens' cooperation.
Reports in foreign media from Monday about the outbreak prompted concern at some foreign embassies in Havana over whether tourists from their countries should visit Santiago.
Santiago is scheduled to host a Caribbean trade fair next week, and Cuban Chamber of Commerce officials have said there is no reason to cancel the event.

Reuters Television cameraman Alfredo Tedeschi said by telephone from Santiago that efforts to eradicate the mosquito were highly visible, with teams of workers fumigating houses and public places such as schools from backpack containers.
Measures to counter the disease focus on killing mosquitoes, fumigation and eliminating stagnant pools of water where the mosquitoes breed.

The weekly trade union newspaper Trabajadores appealed two weeks ago for cooperation in a campaign to eliminate the Aedes Aegypti mosquito, saying the insect was present in parts of Santiago, Havana and the eastern city of Guantanamo. It did not say any cases of dengue had been reported on the island.
